summary: Anaemia means the blood has fewer red cells or less haemoglobin than normal, so the body gets less oxygen. It is very common in India, especially among women, adolescent girls, pregnant women and children. Iron deficiency is the commonest cause, but other causes exist and need to be identified.
causes: Iron deficiency from low dietary iron or blood loss (for example heavy periods)
Worm infection, chronic disease, or inherited conditions such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
Pregnancy increases the body's need for iron
risk_factors: Women of reproductive age, adolescent girls and pregnant women
Diet low in iron, folate or vitamin B12
Chronic illness or long-term blood loss

tests.name: Complete blood count (CBC) with red cell indices
tests.purpose: Measures haemoglobin and red cell size to detect and classify anaemia.

preparation.other: Preparation can differ between labs and between patients; follow the instructions of your doctor or lab.

tests.name: Serum ferritin and iron studies
tests.purpose: Checks whether iron deficiency is the cause.

preparation.fasting: Depends on the lab. Serum iron varies through the day and with recent iron intake, so the lab or doctor may give special instructions.

tests.exceptions: Ferritin can look normal during infection or inflammation even when iron is low; the doctor interprets it with other results. Do not stop prescribed iron without asking the doctor.

tests.name: Vitamin B12 and folate
tests.purpose: Looks for B12 or folate deficiency.
tests.exceptions: Recent supplements can affect results; tell the lab what you take.

tests.name: Peripheral blood smear, haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC
tests.purpose: Looks for inherited blood disorders and other causes.
tests.exceptions: Used when the cause is unclear, anaemia does not respond to treatment, or there is a family history.

prevention: Eat iron-rich foods such as pulses, green leafy vegetables, and (if non-vegetarian) eggs, fish or meat
Include vitamin C-rich foods (such as lemon, amla, citrus fruit) with meals to improve iron absorption
Avoid drinking tea or coffee with meals
Use government-provided iron-folic acid supplements only as advised by a health worker or doctor
lifestyle: Find and treat the cause; taking iron alone without a diagnosis is not advised
Regular check-ups during pregnancy and adolescence
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, chest pain or fainting
Very fast heartbeat with severe weakness
Black stools, blood in stool or vomit
Very heavy periods soaking through pads quickly
Pregnancy with severe tiredness, breathlessness or swelling
when_to_consult: Pregnant women and adolescent girls should have haemoglobin checked as part of routine care
special_populations: Pregnancy: anaemia raises risks for mother and baby; follow antenatal advice
Children: poor appetite, slow growth or frequent illness need paediatric review
Men and post-menopausal women with anaemia need the cause (such as hidden blood loss) checked

faqs.q: Is low haemoglobin always because of low iron?
faqs.a: No. B12 or folate deficiency, chronic disease and inherited conditions are also causes. Tests help find the reason.

faqs.q: Do I need to fast for a haemoglobin test?
faqs.a: No for CBC. Some iron tests may have special instructions; follow your lab.
